subject: print_optim, ancestral states, and example files

messages.author: 665b3d97beb30882
messages.subject: print_optim, ancestral states, and example files
parts:
Replies to a few recent questions:


1. PRINT_OPTIM: PRINTING TO SCREEEN DURING ML OPTIMIZATION


> I was wondering if there is a way to keep the
> optimization from printing out as it runs. I've tried
> print_optim= FALSE, but it continues to print out all
> parameter values and likelihoods for each iteration
> (strangely, only for the DEC and DEC+J analyses).
> Is there
> another command I can use to keep it from printing?


It's the same function for all the models -- the likelihood
versions of DEC, DEC+J, DIVA, DIVA+J, BayArea, BayArea+J are
all special cases of the "BioGeoBEARS supermodel", see:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#toc0


So...print_optim=FALSE should work for anything. Make sure
you do:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$print_optim=FALSE

Probably it is getting reset to TRUE (the default) somewhere
in your script. You can always double-check by typing

BioGeoBEARS_run_object



2. ANCESTRAL STATES (= GEOGRAPHIC RANGES) IN BIOGEOBEARS VS
LAGRANGE

> Also, is
> it possible to call the log likelihood for each ancestral
> range chosen for the plot?

So, BioGeoBEARS and LAGRANGE do ancestral ranges slightly
differently. LAGRANGE does local optimization, i.e. for
every possible ancestral range at every node, it runs an
optimization of the parameters while fixing that range to be
true.

BioGeoBEARS does the (I think) simpler and more intuitive
strategy of just estimating the global optimum parameters,
and then reporting the probabilities of each ancestral state
at each node, under the global model. This is one ML
optimization run. A paper by Mooers (2004) indicates that
ancestral states under the global optimum model may be
slightly more accurate anyway. States estimated by local
optimization may be more formally correct for statistical
hypothesis testing between different ancestral states, but
AFAICT no one ever bothers to do such statistical tests
anyway. So I don't see much point!


If you really want to replicate the exact LAGRANGE ancestral
states in BioGeoBEARS for some reason, you can use the
"fixnode" and "fixlikes" parameters of a
BioGeoBEARS_run_object to fix any node of interest if you
like. To do this for all nodes you would have to do run a
number of ML equal to (# of ranges=# of states) times (# of
nodes). Somehow LAGRANGE does this and makes it run fast
anyway, I assume their ML search is more customized to be
more efficient (I just use an off-the-shelf R package, optimx).


You can see the BioGeoBEARS ancestral state probabilities in
2 ways: they are displayed as pie charts in the example
script, or you can get them all by typing e.g. resDEC
(resDEC= "results of a DEC run", similar for resDECj,
resDIVAj, etc.)



3. EXAMPLE FILES

> I've also been looking in to other systems that I can use as
> examples, but I don't know how to create the .geog and
> .newick files.

The example files are used in the example script you've run,
so if you go through the example script and find the bit
that references those files, you can get the path/filename
and look them up manually, or display them with the moref()
function. I've attached them to the email to help...


> In LAGRANGE, I made them as .txt files and
> imported them into the configurator, so I'm a bit clueless
> as to how to make them for BioGeoBEARS. I've tried changing
> the file extensions to .data and .newick, but the package
> can't read them. I know this might be a dull question, but
> figuring this out would be really helpful!

E.g., "trfn" means "tree filename". This part of the script
references it:

# Input tree
trfn = np(paste(addslash(extdata_dir),
"Psychotria_5.2.newick", sep=""))

To see the full location of the file, type:

trfn

To display the file inside R, type:

moref(trfn)


Same for geogfn. This stuff will become "obvious" once you
get a little more familiar with R, I recommend my little R
phylogenetics tutorial here:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/introduction-to-r

Forgot to add:

I think that print_optim=TRUE is handy to see (a) that it's
actually working (important especially for slow runs,
without this, it will just look like R "freezes" for hours),
and (b) watch how the parameters and log-likelihoods are
being optimized.

But it's a matter of personal preference...if others have
problems turning off print_optim, send me the script/data.

Cheers,
Nick
